title: IC32 Course Chapters & Interactive Study Guide
description: Structured curriculum mapped directly to the official ISA/IEC 62443 Version 6.0 Student Noteset chapters.

chapters.title: Introduction to Control Systems Security
chapters.description: Defining control system cybersecurity, trends, potential consequences, malware events, and differences between IT and IACS.
learningObjectives: Describe the need and importance for control system security
Discuss current trends in control system cybersecurity and how they affect control systems
Analyse the key differences between IT and IACS environments
Recognise common myths regarding cybersecurity in industrial environments

topics.title: Defining Control System Cybersecurity
topics.definition: Cybersecurity is defined as measures taken to protect a computer or computer system against unauthorised access or attack.
topics.beginnerExplanation: In industrial systems, this means electronic security (actions to protect critical industrial assets and networks from unauthorised use, denial of service, modifications, or destruction) applied to hardware and software components of an Industrial Automation and Control System (IACS).
keyPoints: Electronic security protects critical infrastructure from unauthorised use or sabotage
IACS combines physical control hardware/software with people, policies, and processes
Distinction between corporate IT and operational IACS environments
topics.examTip: Remember that IACS security prioritises safety and availability (uptime) above strict confidentiality, unlike standard IT.

topics.title: Trends & Attack Surface in IACS
topics.definition: The evolution of industrial control architectures towards commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) software, standard Internet Protocols (IP), and remote vendor access.
topics.beginnerExplanation: Industrial control systems used to be completely isolated (air-gapped) and used proprietary protocols. Today, they rely on standard Ethernet, Wi-Fi, and Windows/Linux operating systems, which broadens the attack surface and exposes them to internet-borne threats.
keyPoints: Increased use of COTS hardware and software in control rooms
Common adoption of standard IP networking and remote monitoring
Broadened attack surface due to remote vendor access and plant-to-enterprise integration
Proliferation of automated attack tools targeting critical infrastructure
topics.examTip: Air-gapping is increasingly rare or illusory; remote access and corporate network bridges create hidden pathways for malware.

topics.title: Potential Consequences for Organisations & Society
topics.definition: The tangible operational, safety, financial, and societal impacts resulting from an IACS cybersecurity breach.
topics.beginnerExplanation: Unlike IT breaches where data is stolen, an IACS breach can stop a power plant, poison a municipal water supply, cause toxic chemical leaks, or injure plant operators.
keyPoints: Loss of control system availability and operational disruption
Equipment damage and environmental contamination
Personal injury or fatality to plant workers or public
Regulatory non-compliance and reputational damage
topics.examTip: Physical safety (life safety) is always the highest priority when evaluating industrial cybersecurity risks.

chapters.title: Awareness & Training
chapters.description: Explaining the importance of awareness as an effective countermeasure and building role-based security culture.
learningObjectives: Explain the importance of awareness as an effective countermeasure
Describe how to build role-based awareness programmes across organisational tiers
Demonstrate the impact of cyber threats on industrial control systems

topics.title: Awareness as a Countermeasure
topics.definition: Security awareness is the continuous process of educating personnel to recognise and respond to cybersecurity risks.
topics.beginnerExplanation: Technology alone cannot stop attacks. Employees and operators are the human firewall. Giving awareness the same emphasis as physical safety prevents social engineering and inadvertent misconfigurations.
keyPoints: Human error and social engineering remain major threat entry points
Security awareness must match the cultural emphasis placed on plant safety
Ongoing education is required because threat vectors constantly evolve
topics.examTip: Awareness is not a one-time annual event; it must be reinforced regularly and tailored to specific job roles.

topics.title: Executive & Employee Engagement
topics.definition: Tailoring security awareness activities to specific organisational roles, from board members to plant floor operators.
topics.beginnerExplanation: Board members need high-level briefings on business risk and liability, whereas plant operators need practical training on recognising phishing emails and unusual HMI behaviour.
keyPoints: Role-based customisation ensures relevance for plant floor staff vs. executives
High-impact demonstrations (such as malware impact on relay testbeds) drive engagement
Executive leadership must visibly sponsor and participate in security culture
topics.examTip: Executives care about business risk, regulatory compliance, and plant resilience, not technical packet inspection.

chapters.title: ISA/IEC 62443 Series Overview
chapters.definition: The comprehensive international series of standards, technical reports, and specifications for industrial automation cybersecurity.
chapters.description: Structure and content of the ISA/IEC 62443 series across General, Policies & Procedures, System, Component, Profiles, and Evaluation.
learningObjectives: Describe the structure and content of the ISA/IEC 62443 series
Differentiate between Normative Standards, Technical Reports (TR/TS), and PAS
Identify document applicability across Asset Owners, Product Suppliers, and Service Providers

topics.title: Structure of the Series (General to Evaluation)
topics.definition: The ISA/IEC 62443 framework is organised into four distinct horizontal and vertical groups: General (1-x), Policies & Procedures (2-x), System (3-x), and Component (4-x), plus Profiles and Evaluation.
topics.beginnerExplanation: Think of the series as a library: Part 1 gives you the common vocabulary and models, Part 2 gives management policies for plant owners, Part 3 covers plant-wide system architecture, and Part 4 covers how device manufacturers build secure PLCs.
keyPoints: Group 1 (General): Terminology, metrics, and models
Group 2 (Policies & Procedures): Asset owner and service provider programmes
Group 3 (System): Risk assessment, zones, conduits, and system security requirements
Group 4 (Component): Secure product development lifecycle and component technical requirements
topics.examTip: Master the numbering convention: 1-x is General, 2-x is Policies, 3-x is System, 4-x is Component.

topics.title: Document Types: Standards, TS, TR/TS, and PAS
topics.definition: Classification of ISA documents by their normative status and maturity level.
topics.beginnerExplanation: Standards are mandatory normative rules. Technical Specifications (TS) or Technical Reports (TR/TS) provide guidance, use cases, and best practices. Publicly Available Specifications (PAS) offer rapid solutions for urgent industry needs.
keyPoints: Standards: Full consensus normative requirements
TR/TS (Technical Report / Technical Specification): Informative guidance, best practices, and use cases
PAS (Publicly Available Specification): Rapidly published technical specifications for emerging needs
topics.examTip: Standards contain mandatory requirements (using 'shall'), whereas Technical Reports provide guidance (using 'should').

chapters.title: ISA/IEC 62443 Models & Security Levels
chapters.description: The Purdue Reference Model, Zone & Conduit Model, and Security Levels (SL 0-4) with FR vector notation.
learningObjectives: Explain the Purdue Reference Model and its five hierarchical levels
Describe the Zone & Conduit Model, characteristics, and network segmentation
Identify and explain the four Security Levels (SL 1-4) and FR vector notation

topics.title: Purdue Reference Model (Levels 0 to 4)
topics.definition: A hierarchical reference model that categorises industrial automation functions from physical plant floor equipment up to enterprise business networks.
topics.beginnerExplanation: The Purdue model is like a corporate office building: Level 0 is the machinery and sensors in the basement, Level 1 controls them, Level 2 supervises them on the factory floor, Level 3 manages plant operations, and Level 4 handles corporate business and IT.
keyPoints: Level 0 (Process): Physical sensors, actuators, and valves
Level 1 (Basic Control): PLCs, RTUs, and local controllers
Level 2 (Supervisory): SCADA, HMIs, and local operator workstations
Level 3 (Operations): Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES) and plant historians
Level 4 (Enterprise): ERP, corporate IT, and business planning
topics.examTip: Data flows naturally up and down adjacent levels; crossing multiple levels directly (e.g. Level 0 straight to Level 4) creates severe security risks.

topics.title: Zone & Conduit Model (Characteristics & Definitions)
topics.definition: A security architecture approach that groups systems into logical security zones and controls inter-zone communication through secure conduits.
topics.beginnerExplanation: Zones are secure rooms inside a building with locked doors (similar security needs). Conduits are the guarded hallways and tunnels connecting those rooms where traffic is inspected and filtered.
keyPoints: Zones group assets with similar trust levels and security requirements
Conduits are secure communication paths connecting zones with strict traffic filtering
Documenting zones requires defining boundaries, responsible organisations, safety designations, and Target SL
Conduits can be physical (cables) or logical (VLANs, firewalls, VPN tunnels)
topics.examTip: Every industrial asset must belong to either a security zone or a conduit; unclassified assets represent unmitigated risk.

topics.title: Security Levels (SL 0 to SL 4) & FR Vector Notation
topics.definition: A scale representing the target or achieved level of cyber security confidence, defined across seven Foundational Requirements.
topics.beginnerExplanation: Security Levels measure how tough your security is: SL 0 is no security, SL 1 stops casual mistakes, SL 2 stops amateur hackers, SL 3 stops skilled attackers with moderate resources, and SL 4 stops sophisticated nation-state actors.
keyPoints: SL 0: No specific security requirements or baseline
SL 1: Protection against casual or accidental violation
SL 2: Protection against intentional violation using simple means
SL 3: Protection against intentional violation using sophisticated means and moderate resources
SL 4: Protection against intentional violation using sophisticated means and extended resources
FR Vector: SL-T(Zone) = {2, 2, 0, 1, 3, 1, 3} specifying individual levels across the 7 Foundational Requirements
topics.examTip: Security levels are evaluated independently for each of the 7 Foundational Requirements (FR 1 to FR 7) as a vector, not just a single aggregate number.

chapters.title: Introduction to IACS Lifecycle
chapters.description: The continuous cybersecurity lifecycle spanning Assessment, Design, Implementation, Operation, and Maintenance.
learningObjectives: Describe the phases of the IACS cybersecurity lifecycle
Explain how risk assessment drives lifecycle governance
Recognise the importance of continuous maintenance and decommissioning

topics.title: Lifecycle Phases (Assess, Implement, Maintain)
topics.definition: A continuous, cyclical framework for managing IACS cybersecurity from initial concept to final decommissioning.
topics.beginnerExplanation: Cybersecurity isn't a product you buy once; it's a lifecycle. You assess risks, design secure architectures, implement controls, operate safely, and continuously maintain patches and policies.
keyPoints: Phase 1: Security Assessment & Strategy (Risk analysis, policies)
Phase 2: Architecture & Implementation (Zone & Conduit design, deploying firewalls)
Phase 3: Operation & Maintenance (Patch management, monitoring, incident response, auditing)
topics.examTip: The lifecycle is iterative; every plant modification or major upgrade triggers a re-assessment of zones and conduits.

chapters.title: Security Requirements for IACS Asset Owners
chapters.description: Establishing security management systems (CSMS), roles, responsibilities, and protection ratings under 62443-2-1 and 62443-2-2.
learningObjectives: Explain asset owner responsibilities under 62443-2-1
Describe the Cyber Security Management System (CSMS) elements
Apply security protection ratings and governance policies

topics.title: Cyber Security Management System (CSMS)
topics.definition: The overarching policies, procedures, practices, and organisational structures governing industrial cybersecurity for an asset owner.
topics.beginnerExplanation: A CSMS is the company's rulebook and management system for plant security. It ensures that security isn't left to individual technicians but is governed systematically across the entire enterprise.
keyPoints: Asset owner retains ultimate accountability for plant safety and security
CSMS encompasses risk analysis, security policies, training, and incident response
Integration between plant operations (OT) and enterprise security (IT)
topics.examTip: Even when outsourcing maintenance to service providers, the Asset Owner retains ultimate operational accountability.

chapters.title: Evolving Security Standards, Practices & Regulations
chapters.description: Integration of ISA/IEC 62443 with broader regulatory frameworks, NIST CSF, and global compliance mandates.
learningObjectives: Discuss evolving regulations and standards impacting industrial control systems
Compare ISA/IEC 62443 with NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF)
Understand compliance requirements for critical infrastructure operators

topics.title: Regulatory Frameworks & NIST Alignment
topics.definition: The mapping of ISA/IEC 62443 technical requirements to national critical infrastructure regulations and standards.
topics.beginnerExplanation: Governments worldwide mandate critical infrastructure protection. Standards like 62443 provide the engineering blueprint, while frameworks like NIST CSF help organisations manage overall risk.
keyPoints: Mandatory compliance for energy, water, transport, and chemical sectors
Alignment between 62443 (deep engineering control standards) and NIST CSF (management framework)
Auditing and verification of regulatory compliance
topics.examTip: 62443 provides the technical depth for IACS that generic frameworks like NIST or ISO 27001 often omit.

chapters.title: Network Security Basics
chapters.description: Industrial networking principles, OSI model differences in OT, firewalls, and defence-in-depth strategies.
learningObjectives: Explain industrial networking principles and TCP/IP fundamentals
Describe Defence-in-Depth and its application in industrial environments
Configure industrial firewalls and network segmentation

topics.title: Defence-in-Depth & Industrial Segmentation
topics.definition: A security strategy integrating multiple layers of defensive controls so that if one layer fails, subsequent layers protect the system.
topics.beginnerExplanation: Defence-in-depth is like a medieval castle: you have a moat, outer walls, guards at the gate, inner courtyard walls, and locked doors to the treasury. If an attacker climbs the outer wall, they still face multiple interior barriers.
keyPoints: Layered security: physical, network, host, application, and data layers
Network segmentation using industrial firewalls and DMZs (Demilitarised Zones)
Preventing flat networks where a single infected laptop compromises the entire plant floor
topics.examTip: Defence-in-depth ensures that no single security failure (like a compromised firewall) leads to a total plant collapse.

chapters.title: Industrial Protocols
chapters.description: Analysis of legacy and modern industrial communication protocols (Modbus, DNP3, OPC UA, PROFINET) and their security limitations.
learningObjectives: Analyse security characteristics of industrial communication protocols
Identify inherent vulnerabilities in legacy protocols lacking authentication or encryption
Apply protocol-aware filtering and secure tunneling techniques

topics.title: Inherent Protocol Vulnerabilities
topics.definition: The security risks associated with industrial protocols designed for reliability and speed rather than confidentiality and cryptographic authentication.
topics.beginnerExplanation: Traditional protocols like Modbus were designed in the 1970s when networks were physically isolated. They operate on trust: any device can send a command, and the controller executes it without checking who sent it.
keyPoints: Lack of built-in authentication in legacy protocols (anyone can issue write commands)
Absence of encryption (plaintext telemetry and commands can be eavesdropped)
Transition to secure modern protocols (OPC UA, secure DNP3, IEC 62351)
topics.examTip: Legacy protocols cannot be encrypted easily without breaking timing; security must be provided at the network boundary (conduits and firewalls).

chapters.title: Introduction to Patch Management
chapters.description: Structured patch evaluation, testing in staging environments, and safe deployment schedules under 62443-2-3.
learningObjectives: Explain the challenges of patch management in 24/7 industrial environments
Describe the patch management lifecycle under ISA/IEC 62443-2-3
Balance zero-day risk with operational availability during emergency patches

topics.title: Patch Management Lifecycle (62443-2-3)
topics.definition: A structured methodology for assessing, testing, approving, and deploying software and firmware patches in an IACS.
topics.beginnerExplanation: In IT, you patch immediately when a notification arrives. In OT, rebooting a controller or HMI can trip a turbine or shut down a refinery. Patches must be tested in a staging lab that mirrors the live plant before deployment.
keyPoints: Assessment of vendor vulnerability advisories and applicability
Staging lab testing to verify operational stability and real-time performance
Compensating controls (firewall rules, port disabling) when immediate patching is impossible
Emergency patching procedures for critical zero-day exploits
topics.examTip: Availability overrides immediacy; never apply an unverified vendor patch directly to a live production control system.

chapters.title: Introduction to Security Risk Assessment for System Design
chapters.description: Cybersecurity risk assessment methodology (62443-3-2), identifying System Under Consideration (SuC), threat modelling, and determining Target Security Levels.
learningObjectives: Describe the risk assessment process under ISA/IEC 62443-3-2
Define the System Under Consideration (SuC) and partition into zones and conduits
Perform threat modelling and determine Target Security Levels (SL-T)

topics.title: Risk Assessment & System Under Consideration (SuC)
topics.definition: The formal process of identifying assets, vulnerabilities, threat sources, and potential consequences to establish security requirements.
topics.beginnerExplanation: Before you can secure a plant, you must draw a box around what you are securing (the System Under Consideration), identify what can go wrong, how likely it is, and what the impact would be.
keyPoints: Defining the System Under Consideration (SuC) and its boundaries
Partitioning the SuC into security zones and conduits
Evaluating threat sources, attack paths, and worst-case consequences
Establishing Target Security Levels (SL-T) based on risk tolerance
topics.examTip: Risk assessment is the anchor of the entire 62443 framework; technical controls are chosen specifically to close the gap between Achieved and Target Security Levels.

chapters.title: Security Programme Requirements for IACS Service Providers
chapters.description: Mandatory security requirements for third-party integrators, contractors, and maintenance vendors under 62443-2-4.
learningObjectives: Explain the security obligations of third-party service providers under 62443-2-4
Evaluate service provider security capabilities and contractual requirements
Manage secure remote access for vendors and integrators

topics.title: Service Provider Requirements (62443-2-4)
topics.definition: Requirements for integration, maintenance, and support services provided by third parties to asset owners.
topics.beginnerExplanation: Many plants rely on outside vendors for maintenance and programming. Part 2-4 ensures that external vendors don't bring infected laptops into the plant or create unmonitored backdoor connections.
keyPoints: Mandatory security competency for system integrators and maintenance contractors
Securing vendor remote access (bastion hosts, multi-factor authentication, session logging)
Contractual alignment with asset owner CSMS policies
topics.examTip: Third-party remote access is one of the most common vectors for industrial cyberattacks; 62443-2-4 governs how this risk is mitigated.

chapters.title: Developing Secure Products & Systems
chapters.description: Secure Product Development Lifecycle (SDLC) under 62443-4-1 and technical component requirements under 62443-4-2.
learningObjectives: Describe the Secure Product Development Lifecycle (SDLC) requirements under 62443-4-1
Explain technical security requirements for IACS components under 62443-4-2
Evaluate component security capabilities (embedded devices, host devices, networks, software)

topics.title: Secure Product Development Lifecycle (62443-4-1)
topics.definition: Mandatory security practices across every phase of product creation, from security requirements gathering to vulnerability management and retirement.
topics.beginnerExplanation: Device manufacturers can't just bolt security on at the end. Part 4-1 requires them to design security into PLCs and sensors from day one, including threat modelling, secure coding standards, and vulnerability handling.
keyPoints: Security requirements definition and threat modelling during design
Secure coding practices and peer code reviews
Vulnerability handling process for reporting and issuing firmware fixes
Security verification and penetration testing before product release
topics.examTip: 62443-4-1 applies to the *process* the manufacturer uses, whereas 62443-4-2 specifies the *technical features* of the final product.

topics.title: Component Technical Requirements (62443-4-2)
topics.definition: Technical security requirements for four component types: embedded devices, host devices, network components, and software applications.
topics.beginnerExplanation: Part 4-2 provides the technical checklist for a PLC or HMI: does it support unique user accounts? Does it encrypt configuration uploads? Does it disable unused communication ports?
keyPoints: Embedded devices (PLCs, RTUs, smart sensors)
Host devices (engineering workstations, HMI servers)
Network components (industrial switches, firewalls, routers)
Software applications (SCADA packages, historian software)
topics.examTip: Component security requirements are mapped directly to the 7 Foundational Requirements (FR 1 to FR 7).

chapters.title: Security Profiles for ISA 62443
chapters.description: Tailoring 62443 standards for specific industrial domains and sectors (e.g., Electric Energy OT, Oil & Gas).
learningObjectives: Explain how security profiles tailor generic 62443 standards to specific industries
Describe domain-specific security challenges in electric power, oil & gas, and manufacturing
Utilise security profiles during system design and procurement

topics.title: Industry Security Profiles (62443-5-x)
topics.definition: Pre-tailored subsets of 62443 requirements adapted for specific vertical industrial sectors.
topics.beginnerExplanation: A nuclear power plant, an offshore oil rig, and a pharmaceutical factory all use 62443, but their exact priorities differ. Security profiles provide pre-packaged guidance for specific industries.
keyPoints: Tailoring general requirements for sector-specific regulatory and physical constraints
Electric Energy OT profiles (aligned with NERC CIP and IEC standards)
Oil & Gas sector security profiles for upstream and downstream facilities
topics.examTip: Profiles save engineering time by providing pre-selected security levels and baseline controls for specific industries.

chapters.title: IACS Security Profile Scheme
chapters.description: Establishing frameworks and conformity schemes for evaluating and certifying industrial security profiles.
learningObjectives: Describe the scheme and methodology for 62443 cybersecurity profiles
Understand conformance assessment and certification principles
Course wrap-up and certification requirements review

topics.title: Profile Scheme & Conformance Assessment
topics.definition: The overarching mechanism for verifying that products, systems, and programmes conform to ISA/IEC 62443 requirements.
topics.beginnerExplanation: How do you know a PLC is really 62443 compliant? Independent certification schemes (like ISASecure) test and certify products against 4-1 and 4-2 standards.
keyPoints: Third-party certification and testing laboratories
ISASecure component and system certifications
Conformity assessment methodologies for asset owners and service providers
topics.examTip: Certification provides objective proof of security compliance during procurement and regulatory audits.
